To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the security of a multi-factor authentication protocol can be reduced to the security of its device pairing sub-protocol; that the latter can be analysed by a formal model of the actor-networks, where the protocol runs, and the formal methods that we have developed for reasoning about the protocols in these actor-networks; and that the security of the actor-network can be reduced to that of its social network.

1) actor-network procedures are the software connectors for modern, world wide, computational and social software systems, and 2) they can be modeled and reasoned about using the formalism of Procedure Derivation Logic.
security protocols can be seen as a special case of procedures that run in actor-networks, and that the logic for reasoning about protocols can be extended to reason about procedures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a formalism that can be used to design and reason about security procedures in heterogenous networks.
the development of a formal framework and tools for reasoning about the security of multi-factor authentication protocols and other procedures for securing networks of computers, devices and humans.
the formalization of security protocols and procedures, their derivation from specifications, and their verification.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

actor-networks and PDL provide the formal basis for the design of procedures for multi-factor authentication, secure pairing of mobile devices, social interaction protocols, and other security tasks in heterogenous networks.
actor-network procedures can be modeled in PDL, and vice versa.
the new procedures for security in heterogeneous networks, and the new logic for reasoning about them are still under development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
actor-networks are the computational substrate for procedures, that are a generalization of protocols.
we have developed a new approach to security protocols and their reasoning that is based on a formalization of the idea that security protocols are procedures, and that procedures are programs.
the security of a computational system depends on the security of the software procedures that run in it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the formalisms of security protocols and procedural programming can be integrated to form a new formalism for programming of global behaviors in heterogenous networks.
the new security protocols, or procedures, are more than just protocols, they are procedures in the procedural sense, and they are best modelled by actor networks.
the new discipline of security programming is a generalization of the established discipline of security protocols.
